narration: The average American wedding now costs around thirty-three thousand dollars — a house down payment, spent on a single day. In some states it's over fifty thousand; in others, half that. But here's the twist nobody at the bridal shop will tell you: the research says the more you spend on the wedding, the higher your odds of divorce. Today we rank what a wedding costs in every state — and what it should.

narration: Here's the number that should give every engaged couple pause. A single wedding day, in the priciest states, can cost over fifty thousand dollars — more than many Americans earn in a year. It's one of the largest discretionary purchases a person will ever make, and it buys something that's over in about six hours.
sub: average US wedding — for one day

narration: So today we rank wedding costs across the states, break down where all that money actually goes, expose the psychology and the industry quietly inflating the bill, reveal what the data says about spending and lasting marriages, and show what a wedding should really cost. Because few expenses blend love, pressure, and financial logic quite as messily as this one.

memeTop: spend big to show how much you love them
memeBottom: spend less and start the marriage richer
narration: Because a wedding is where emotion and money collide hardest — and the story the industry sells, that bigger means more love, turns out to be exactly backwards. Before we rank the states, let's separate the wedding from the marriage.
First, the crucial difference between a wedding and a marriage.
heading: Wedding vs Marriage

narration: A wedding is a ceremony in which two people are united in marriage. That's it — a ceremony, a single event. Everything beyond the legal act of marrying is optional: the venue, the guests, the band, the three-tiered cake. We've bundled an enormous, expensive party onto what is, at its core, a short ceremony and a signature.

And the modern 'traditional' wedding is younger than you think. The white dress, the diamond ring, the enormous reception — much of it was invented or supercharged by twentieth-century marketing, not ancient custom. The diamond engagement ring, famously, was a jewelry-industry campaign. A lot of what feels like timeless obligation is really advertising that worked a little too well.

The thing that actually lasts is marriage — a culturally and often legally recognised union between people called spouses. The marriage is the decades; the wedding is the afternoon. Yet couples routinely pour a year's income and months of stress into the afternoon, while investing almost nothing in preparing for the decades. We spend on the party and wing the partnership.

And this split explains the strange grief many couples feel after the wedding. They poured a year of energy and savings into one afternoon, and then it's simply over — and the actual marriage, the hard and beautiful part, begins with a drained bank account. We front-load all the investment into the easy day and arrive at the hard decades empty-handed.

Here's the proportion that should stop couples cold. The legal act of getting married — the license and the officiant — typically costs a couple hundred dollars at most. Everything else, the other ninety-nine percent of a thirty-three-thousand-dollar wedding, is an optional party. You are not required to spend any of it to be just as married.
sub: of a wedding's cost is optional party, not marriage

narration: So the real question isn't how much a wedding costs — it's what you're actually buying. A legal marriage costs almost nothing: a license fee, often under a hundred dollars. Everything on top is a party, and a party's price is entirely a choice. The thirty-three-thousand-dollar average isn't the cost of getting married. It's the cost of the celebration we decided getting married requires.

Put the opportunity cost in focus. Thirty-three thousand dollars invested instead of spent, growing over a thirty-year marriage, becomes well over two hundred thousand dollars. The real price of the average wedding isn't the thirty-three thousand. It's the quarter-million in retirement the couple quietly chose a party over.
sub: what an average wedding could have grown into

narration: And the ring deserves its own reality check. The 'spend two months' salary' rule wasn't ancient wisdom — it was a jewelry marketing slogan, full stop. There's no law of love that sets a diamond's price. Couples spend thousands on a ring precisely because an ad campaign, decades ago, told them that's what commitment looks like. The tradition is real; its origin is a billboard.
So let's rank what a wedding costs by state.
heading: The Ranking

narration: One honest note on these state numbers: averages are dragged upward by lavish, high-end weddings. The typical couple often spends less than the headline average suggests, and plenty marry happily for a few thousand dollars. So don't read the state figure as a target you must hit. Read it as proof of how far the normal has drifted from the necessary.

caption: average wedding cost, by state
narration: Here's the wedding leaderboard. In lower-cost states like Utah and much of the Mountain West and South, the average runs around twenty thousand dollars. The coasts climb fast. And in the Northeast — New York, New Jersey, Massachusetts — the average soars past fifty thousand, driven by pricey venues, big guest lists, and sky-high local costs. The same two people, the same vows, double the bill by geography.

And notice the pricey states aren't pricey because couples there love more — it's the same venue-and-vendor cost of living we keep finding. A Manhattan ballroom and a Nebraska barn host the identical vows, but one charges Manhattan prices. The geography of weddings is really just the geography of real estate and labor, wearing a tuxedo.

title: Average wedding cost ($K)
narration: Put the numbers in a row. Utah around twenty thousand, Texas twenty-eight, Florida thirty-two, California thirty-eight, New York forty-eight, and New Jersey leading near fifty-three. The gap between the cheapest and priciest state is over thirty thousand dollars — the difference, quite literally, between starting your marriage with a car or with a house deposit in the bank.

And weddings suffer from a special kind of markup. Tell a vendor an event is a wedding, and quotes mysteriously rise — the same flowers, catering, or venue often cost noticeably more under the word 'wedding' than 'party.' The industry knows couples are emotional, time-pressured, and spending once in a lifetime. That combination is a pricing dream, and the bill reflects it.

caption: where the wedding money goes
narration: And here's where all that money actually goes. The single biggest slice, by far, is the venue and catering — feeding and seating your guests can be half the entire budget. Then the ring, photography, attire, flowers, music, and a hundred small line items. The guest list is the hidden master dial: every extra head adds to catering, space, and favors. Invite fewer people, and almost everything shrinks at once.

memeBottom: a small wedding and a house deposit
narration: This is the single most expensive decision in the whole budget: the guest list. Every name you add multiplies across catering, seating, drinks, and favors. Cutting the list isn't cutting love — it's the fastest, least painful way to turn a fifty-thousand-dollar wedding into a twenty-thousand-dollar one, with the people who actually matter still in the room.
So why do we spend so wildly on a single day?
heading: The Pressure

narration: And there's a deep psychological trap called the sunk-prestige escalation. Once you book a nice venue, everything else must 'match' it — you can't put cheap flowers in a grand hall, or a budget dress against a designer backdrop. One upscale choice silently drags the entire budget up to its level. The expensive wedding isn't one big decision. It's a hundred small ones, each justified by the last.

A huge part of it is keeping up with the Joneses, where the neighbor serves as a benchmark for social class. Weddings are intensely public, compared, and now broadcast on social media. Couples benchmark against the lavish weddings they've attended and scrolled past, and quietly feel theirs must match. The bill balloons not from their own desires, but from the fear of falling short of everyone else's.

And social media poured rocket fuel on all of it. Weddings are now content — photographed, posted, and compared against an endless feed of other people's highlight reels. Couples don't just host a wedding; they produce one for an audience that was never invited. That invisible pressure to be post-worthy has quietly added thousands to the modern wedding bill.

And parents and family can quietly inflate the whole thing. Who pays, who's invited, whose traditions are honored — each person added to the decision adds pressure and cost. A wedding that started as two people's celebration can balloon into a family political summit, with the budget as collateral damage. Protecting your number sometimes means protecting it from the people who love you most.

It tips into conspicuous consumption — the consumer practice of buying and using goods of a higher quality or price than practical, specifically to signal status. A wedding is the ultimate stage for it: a public, once-in-a-lifetime chance to display taste and success. The open bar, the designer dress, the destination venue — much of it isn't for the couple's joy. It's a performance for the audience.

And the cruelest trap is that the pressure often comes from love, not vanity. Parents want to show pride, couples want to honor their guests, nobody wants to seem cheap about something this meaningful. The wedding industry is brilliant precisely because it weaponizes generosity. Spending more feels like caring more — which is exactly the illusion that empties the bank account.
And now the finding the wedding industry really doesn't want you to hear.
heading: Cost vs Marriage

memeTop: $40,000 in wedding debt, honeymoon on a credit card
narration: For too many newlyweds, this is the real morning after: not the joy of a marriage beginning, but the dawn of a debt that will shadow its first years. Starting a life together while digging out of a hole you dug for a single party is a brutal, avoidable way to begin.

caption: spend more, divorce more
narration: Here's the twist. Researchers studying thousands of marriages found that, if anything, higher wedding spending is associated with a higher chance of divorce, not a lower one. Couples who spent the most on the ring and the wedding were more likely to split, while those who kept it modest tended to last. The expensive wedding isn't buying a stronger marriage. Sometimes it's quietly predicting a weaker one.

Here's the study that reframes everything. Economists who tracked thousands of couples found those who spent the most on their weddings were among the most likely to divorce, while those who spent modestly, and had many guests but a cheap celebration, tended to last longest. Big crowd, small price was the winning combination — not a lavish, expensive show.

And it makes sense once you think about it. Starting a marriage with crushing debt or a drained savings account imports financial stress into the relationship from day one — and money fights are a leading cause of divorce. A giant wedding can literally fund its own undoing. Meanwhile, the couples who resisted the pressure often started richer, calmer, and on the same financial page.

This doesn't mean a cheap wedding guarantees a happy marriage — correlation isn't destiny. But it shatters the core sales pitch: that a more expensive wedding is a more serious, more loving, more lasting one. At best, the money makes no difference to the marriage. At worst, the debt and stress it creates actively work against it. Either way, the big spend buys you nothing that lasts.

Flip the whole thing into a head start. Take even half of an average wedding budget — say fifteen thousand dollars — put it toward a home down payment or investments, and you've turned the most forgettable kind of spending into the foundation of a life. The best wedding gift a couple can give themselves is the one they don't spend.
sub: redirected into a home or investments

narration: So what should a wedding actually cost?
heading: What To Do

narration: And consider the quietly radical option: a tiny wedding, or eloping, then a bigger party later if you want one. Many couples who skipped the giant production report zero regret and a five-figure head start on their marriage. The fear is that you'll wish you'd done more. The reality, over and over, is that people wish they'd spent less and stressed less.

Most of the budget is the wedding reception — a party held after the ceremony as hospitality for those who attended. So that's where the real savings live. A smaller guest list, an off-peak date, a non-traditional venue, and skipping the status add-ons can cut a wedding by half or more without touching anything that actually matters to the couple. The ceremony is sacred; the party is negotiable.

And watch the sneaky budget-killers that add up fast. The open bar, the plus-ones, the Saturday-in-June premium, the elaborate florals that die by Monday, the save-the-dates and favors nobody keeps. None of these are what your guests will actually remember — they remember the people, the food, and the feeling. Cutting the forgettable extras is painless, and it's where the real money hides.

So decide your number first, as a couple, before anyone else weighs in — and protect it. Spend lavishly on the two or three things you'll genuinely remember, and ruthlessly cut the rest that's really there to impress guests. And take whatever you save and pour it into the marriage: a home, an emergency fund, a honeymoon you're not paying off for years. Start the life, don't just stage the day.

props.name: house
props.label: invest the rest in the life

narration: And here's a reframe that quietly saves marriages, not just money: spend a fraction of the wedding budget on actually preparing for marriage. A few sessions of premarital counseling, honest conversations about money, kids, and expectations — the things that genuinely predict whether a marriage lasts. It's the least glamorous line item imaginable, and by far the highest-return one.

Because here's the real lesson. A wedding is one day; a marriage is the rest of your life — and the data is clear that spending more on the first does nothing to protect the second. The couples who win aren't the ones with the grandest party. They're the ones who refused to confuse the cost of a celebration with the strength of a commitment. Celebrate fully. Just don't mortgage the marriage to do it.

And zoom out on what the wedding bill really measures. It's a near-perfect lab for every money lesson there is: social pressure, status signaling, the industry's markup, and the gap between what feels necessary and what actually is. Master your thinking here — on the most emotional purchase of your life — and you'll make calmer, clearer money decisions about everything that comes after it.
